A report to the library board on the orchard partnership

The neighborhood orchard group would like to thank the library board for its support over the past year and to share a short report on how the partnership has gone. We also want to lay out a few proposals for the coming year, which we hope the board will consider at its spring meeting.

As the board knows, the orchard sits on the empty lot directly behind the library building. When we first approached the library about using the space, there were reasonable concerns about liability, maintenance, and how the orchard would look from the reading room windows. We think the first year has gone well on all three counts, and we want to explain why.

On liability, the group took out a small insurance policy through a regional network of community gardens. The policy covers volunteer injuries and any damage the orchard might cause to library property. There have been no claims this year. We have also kept a simple safety rule in place for every work day, which is that power tools are only used by trained volunteers and only while a second adult is present. We plan to keep that rule going forward.

On maintenance, the volunteers have kept the lot mowed, cleared, and free of litter throughout the year. Several library staff members have told us that the space looks better now than it did when it was an empty lawn. We also cleaned out the old storm drain at the edge of the lot, which had been blocked for years and was causing water to pool near the back entrance of the library. The maintenance staff noticed the difference after the first heavy rain.

On appearance, we know that young fruit trees are not much to look at in their first year, and we appreciate the board's patience. The trees now have a full season of growth behind them, and the flower border we planted along the edge of the lot was in bloom from June through September. Several patrons have stopped volunteers to ask what we are growing and how they can help. We have added a small number of them to our mailing list, and a few have become regular volunteers.

We would also like to report on the joint programs the orchard and the library ran this year. In the summer, a children's librarian led three story hours in the orchard, sitting in the shade at the edge of the lot. Attendance was strong, and the librarian has asked whether we could do more next year. In the fall, we held a small cider evening in the library's community room, which raised money for the orchard's new fence. We were glad to see many library regulars there, along with orchard volunteers and neighbors who had not been involved with either before.

Now to our proposals for the coming year.

First, we would like the board's permission to build a small tool shed near the gate on the library side of the lot. A volunteer carpenter has drawn a simple design, about eight feet by six, with a sloped roof and a locking door. The shed would be built by volunteers and maintained by the orchard group. We have checked with the city, and a structure of that size does not need a building permit, but it does need the landowner's written consent. We have attached the design for the board to review.

Second, we would like to expand the joint programs. We propose a monthly series of outdoor story hours from May through September, along with a pruning workshop in the spring that would be listed on the library calendar and open to all patrons. We also want to work toward a seed library, a small cabinet in the library lobby where patrons could borrow and return seeds, with the orchard volunteers helping to stock it. Many libraries around the country have started seed libraries in recent years, and they have proved popular.

Third, we would like to discuss a longer agreement. Our current arrangement with the library is a one-year letter of understanding. Fruit trees take several years to mature, and the volunteers who have given so much time this year would feel more secure with a longer commitment. We would propose a five-year agreement, with a review each year and a clear process for either side to end it with reasonable notice. We would be happy to work with the library's counsel on the terms.

We want to be honest about the challenges as well. The deer damage in late summer set several trees back, and our temporary fence is not a long-term answer. We are raising money for a permanent fence, and we expect to install it in the spring. We also lost four trees in a wet corner of the lot, and we are replanting that area with varieties better suited to damp ground. We will analyze how those trees do and report back to the board next year.

We have also learned a good deal about our own organization. Our volunteer base is smaller than the number of people who first signed up, but it is steady and committed. We have learned to keep work days short and well planned, to give volunteers clear ownership of specific trees and tasks, and to welcome newcomers properly. While there is always more to do, we feel the group is in a stronger position now than at any point since we started.

Finally, we want to say something about why this partnership matters to us. A library is one of the few places in a neighborhood where anyone can walk in, stay as long as they like, and leave having learned something, without paying a cent. We think an orchard can be a little like that. Anyone can walk through it, sit for a while, and over time, pick a piece of fruit. The two fit together naturally, and we are grateful that the library has been willing to try the idea with us.

Thank you again for your support. We would be glad to meet with the board or with any members who would like to walk the orchard and see the work for themselves. The trees are dormant now, but there is still plenty to see, and the volunteers would be happy to show you around. We look forward to working with the library over the coming year, and we hope to keep moving toward an orchard the whole neighborhood can enjoy.

Respectfully submitted on behalf of the orchard steering group, with thanks to every volunteer who made the first year possible, and to the library staff who answered our many questions with patience and good humor.
